summary:
Queensland sits within the Australian federal framework. The federal Sex Discrimination Act has protected gender identity since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that gender-identity discrimination protection extends to trans women as women, and awarded compensation against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member; the case arose out of organised exclusionary activism and stands as national precedent on access to services under sex-discrimination law.

There are no laws in Australia confining bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held since 2017, which matters to same-sex couples arriving together. State law in Queensland has moved in the protective direction on several fronts: same-sex conduct was decriminalised in the 1990s reforms, and rights have broadly advanced in line with the national standard.

Queensland enacted the country's first criminal ban on conversion practices, with the Health Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 passing on 13 August 2020. Practices including electro-shock, drug and hypnotherapy aimed at changing a person's sexuality or gender identity are criminalised, with fines and jail time for practitioners. Survivors have told SBS the ban does not reach conversion practices carried out in informal, non-healthcare settings.

Anti-discrimination law was rewritten with amendments commencing on 29 April 2024. The Queensland Human Rights Commission describes a modernised gender identity attribute, protection extended explicitly to non-binary and gender-diverse people, and a broadened definition of gender identity. Serious vilification moved from the Anti-Discrimination Act into the Criminal Code, raising the maximum penalty from six months to three years' imprisonment.

The sharpest adverse measure for a visitor concerns access to care. Since January 2025 new public-system patients under 18 with gender dysphoria are barred from puberty blockers and hormone therapy under a Queensland Health directive dated 28 January 2025, issued under Health Minister Tim Nicholls, which exempts existing patients of the Queensland Children's Gender Service. The ban remains legally contested. Equality Australia has described Queensland as an outlier state.

Detention carries the sharpest residual physical risk. A 2009 Queensland corrective services procedure on transgender prisoners was assessed as largely ineffective; oversight passed to the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, fully in force from 2023, and inspection standards issued in August 2023 for Queensland prisons and youth detention centres direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender. Placement is therefore identity-based, with a discretionary admission caveat and an exception tied to sexual reassignment surgery.
tangentialFactors:
Queensland contrasts with New South Wales, which passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024, and with other states that have not imposed comparable restrictions on trans youth healthcare. Equality Australia's characterisation of Queensland as an outlier state refers specifically to the under-18 public-system treatment ban, not to the anti-discrimination regime, which has been strengthened in line with the national direction.

The national environment is contested rather than uniformly supportive. ANROWS research maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender diverse rights in Australia, naming organised exclusionary campaigns, disputes over access to facilities and records, and pressure to roll back existing rights; the same research documents systemic discrimination and harassment experienced by trans people. The Tickle case grew out of precisely this kind of organised exclusionary activism, even though the court's finding favoured protection.

Healthcare costs fall on individuals while the public-system ban is contested. Affected families report private treatment costs of hundreds of dollars per injection, with nearly $2,000 reported in one case. This creates a practical divide between trans visitors who can fund private care and those who cannot.

outOfScopeNotes:
The legal challenge to the under-18 public-system treatment ban is unresolved in the available sources. The outcome, timetable and any interim relief are not stated, and whether the directive will be amended, extended to other jurisdictions' pathways, or withdrawn is not sourced here.

How the Criminal Code vilification offence is investigated and charged in practice is not documented in this inventory; the penalty ceiling is sourced, enforcement rates are not. The same gap applies to the conversion practices ban: coverage of informal non-healthcare settings is reported as absent, but prosecution volumes and complaint-handling outcomes are not.

The precise wording of the sexual reassignment surgery exception in the Queensland inspection standards, and the frequency with which the discretionary admission caveat is exercised, are not sourced. Detention-placement outcomes for trans visitors or new remandees during the current window are likewise not documented.

The quantum of compensation awarded in Tickle v Giggle and the specific contractual and statutory provisions relied on are not detailed in the available sources; only the finding and the general characterisation as a national precedent are on record.
